extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers of classical mechanics / natural philosophy (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: A sequence of classical propositions on motion under centripetal forces: apsidal motion of nearly circular orbits, motion in planes and on curved surfaces, cycloid pendulums and isochronous motion, and methods to compute times and velocities for such motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apsidal motion for nearly circular orbits (Prop. XLV, Prob. XXXI)
rubrics_metrics.description: For orbits that are nearly circular, find the motion of the apsides by comparing the centripetal forces that produce the orbit described by a body moving in an ellipse while the surrounding plane is immobile versus the body moving in an ellipse while the plane (or the orbit) itself revolves. Using series expansion of the numerator in A (altitude) and letting the orbit approach a circle, one obtains limiting ratios that determine the angle between successive apsides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: express the centripetal force as a function with denominator A^3 and expand the numerator (e.g., (T - X)^n) in a convergent series; compare corresponding terms (given vs non-given) and take the circular limit (R, T equal and X → 0) to obtain proportions between relevant quantities (G and F in the text). Examples show special force laws (constant force, power laws A^{n-3}, linear combinations bA^m + cA^n) and yield closed-form relations for the apsidal angle (e.g., for force ∝ A^{n-3}, the apsidal angle between extrema is 180/√n degrees). The exposition includes worked Examples 1–3 deriving specific formulae and numerical consequences (e.g., uniform centripetal force gives an apsidal angle ≈ 103°55').

rubrics_metrics.name: Deduce/construct centripetal power-law from observed apsidal motion (Corollary 1 to Prop. XLV)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the total angular motion of the body between returns to the same apside is in a fixed ratio m:n to a full 360° revolution, then the centripetal force varies as A^{(n n ÷ m m) - 3}; conversely, the observed apsidal motion determines the exponent of the altitude in the centripetal force law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the relation derived in the examples: when the angular motion between apsides in the elliptical (immobile) case is 180°, the apsidal angle in the nearly circular orbit under a centripetal law proportional to A^{p} gives p related to (nn ÷ mm) - 3. The corollary lists consequences for various m:n ratios (e.g., m:n = 1:1 yields force ∝ 1/A^2). It also gives qualitative behavior depending on whether the exponent makes the force decrease faster or slower than the cube of the altitude (e.g., if force falls faster than A^3, bodies fall to center or escape to infinity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of adding an external centripetal term to inverse-square law (Corollary 2 to Prop. XLV)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the main centripetal force is inverse-square (1/A^2) and an extra centripetal term (proportional to A, or more generally any additional term) is added or removed, the resulting apsidal motion can be computed via the example-series method (Example 3) and yields a modified apsidal angle given by explicit algebraic expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if original force is 1/A^2 and an external term cA is subtracted (so resultant ~ (A - cA^4)/A^3), the method of series expansion (Example 3) with T normalized to 1 gives formulae for the apsidal angle: e.g., angle = 180 * sqrt{(1 - c)/(1 - 4c)}. A numeric illustration shows how small perturbing forces shift apsidal advance per revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: General result: motion with any centripetal force in a given plane (Prop. XLVI, Prob. XXXII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any centripetal force (of any lawful form), a centre of forces, and a given plane in which a body departs from a given point with a given rectilinear velocity, the trajectory of the body in that plane and its motion are determinable (provided quadratures of the relevant curves are available).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: resolve the centripetal force into components relative to the plane; one component perpendicular to the plane does not alter the motion in the plane, while the in-plane component acts like a centripetal force about some point C in the plane; then apply earlier propositions (e.g., Prop. XLII) to find the curve, locus at given times, and velocity. The proposition reduces motion in non-horizontal geometries to an equivalent planar central-force problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: If centripetal force ∝ distance → planar orbits are ellipses with equal-period revolutions (Prop. XLVII, Theor. XV)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the centripetal force is proportional to the distance from the center (SV ∝ SQ), all bodies moving in any plane about that center describe ellipses and complete their revolutions in equal times; bodies moving in straight lines through the center traverse out-and-back in equal times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: resolve the force and show the in-plane effective centripetal component is proportional to the distance CQ in that plane; hence the same linear restoring law applies in every plane, leading to harmonic motion with closed elliptical orbits and equal-periodness (analogous to Hooke's law).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rolling wheel on a sphere: length of trochoidal path (Prop. XLVIII, Theor. XVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a wheel rolls externally (contacts at right angles) on a globe and rolls along a great circle so that the contact point moves with the wheel's rotation, then the length of the curvilinear path traced by a fixed point on the rim is to twice the sine-versed arc of half the wheel-arc (between successive contacts) as the sum of the diameters of the globe and the wheel is to the globe's semidiameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric construction: compare infinitesimal increments and use similarity of vanishing figures; deduce that AP (the traced path) : 2 sin(½ arc PB) = 2CE : CB (CE semiradius of globe, CB semiradius of wheel). Corollaries give relations for cycloid lengths and semiperimeter relations important later in pendulum constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rolling wheel inside a globe: inner cycloid length relation (Prop. XLIX, Theor. XVII)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a wheel rolling inside (concave contact) a sphere along a great circle, the length of the curvilinear path traced by a fixed rim point is to twice the sine-versed half-arc as the difference of diameters of globe and wheel is to the globe semidiameter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same infinitesimal geometric-similarity reasoning as the external rolling case; corollaries: (1) if the cycloid is bisected, PS:VP has a given ratio; (2) semiperimeter of the cycloid relates to a straight line proportional to the wheel diameter and globe semidiameter; (3) the semiperimeter equals a rectangle (BEC) if the globe semidiameter is given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct a pendulum that oscillates in a given cycloid (Prop. L, Prob. XXXIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a cycloid arc inside a sphere (with its endpoints on the sphere), construct an external semicycloid and a hanging pendulum of a certain length so that the pendulum bob oscillates along the given cycloid arc. The construction uses similarity of arcs and specific choice of the pendulum length equal to a chord/arc relation (AR equals the half-cycloid arc APS).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: bisect the given cycloid arc, erect particular similar constructions (centers and circles) to obtain an outer semicycloid whose half-arc equals the pendulum length; suspend a bob from the constructed point with string length equal to that half-arc. The proof verifies via geometry that the bob's string is always tangent where required and the bob follows the given cycloid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isochronous oscillations for cycloidal pendulum under central force ∝ distance (Prop. LI, Theor. XVIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the centripetal force acting towards the globe's center is proportional to the distance from the center and that force alone causes a mass to oscillate along the perimeter cycloid (constructed as above), then all oscillations (however unequal in amplitude) have equal times — i.e., they are isochronous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decompose the central force into components parallel and perpendicular to the tangent; the tangential accelerating component is proportional to the arc to be traversed, hence accelerations, velocities, and remaining arcs all scale in the same proportion and bodies released simultaneously arrive simultaneously. The argument also shows symmetry between ascent and descent and equal times for corresponding arcs; used to justify tautochrone property of cycloid pendulums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute pendulum velocities and times from given data (Prop. LII, Prob. XXXIV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a cycloid and a pendulum constrained to it (with central force proportional to distance), one can define velocities at each point and the times for whole oscillations and parts of oscillations. The proposition gives constructions: relate arcs and semicircles, set up auxiliary semicircles and use similarity to express velocities and times in terms of given geometric lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: with chosen center G and semicircle GH of radius GK such that GH equals the cycloid semi-arc RS, relate the time for arc ST to the time for full oscillation by proportions of arcs and semicircle lengths; velocity at a point T relates to the velocity at the lowest point R as the ordinate LI to radius GK, i.e., as sqrt(SR^2 - TR^2) : SR. Corollaries generalize to comparing oscillation times across different cycloids and globes and include the limit to planar cycloid pendulums (Wren, Huygens results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Given a curved path, find centripetal forces that make oscillations isochronous (Prop. LIII, Prob. XXXV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an arbitrary curved line (with axis through the center of forces), there exists a centripetal force law (a function proportional to a chosen perpendicular from the body to the axis) such that a mass constrained to the curve oscillates isochronously — all oscillations take equal time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: at any point T choose a tangent TX and take a segment TY equal to the arc TR. The required centripetal force at T is proportional to the perpendicular TZ to the axis (i.e., the projection giving TZ). Thus the force law is obtained from the geometry of the curve and the desired equality TY = TR. Corollaries: for a circular arc with an added uniform downward force proportional to a sine, one recovers classical isochronous conditions relevant for clocks; practical use in clockmaking is noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute descent/ascent times along any plane curve under arbitrary centripetal force (Prop. LIV, Prob. XXXVI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any centripetal force law and any planar curve through the centre, the time to descend or ascend along that curve from one point to another can be computed by dividing the radial distance into infinitesimal segments, constructing corresponding concentric circles, and integrating (quadrature) the local time contributions proportional to small chord lengths divided by velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: partition CS into many equal parts, draw circles at those radii cutting the curve, use Prop. XXXIX to obtain velocity at each altitude CT, and integrate the local time element (proportional to infinitesimal arc length / velocity). The result: the required time is obtained from the area of a constructed curve SNDS (an auxiliary 'area' curve) proportional to elapsed time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area swept by a parallel on a curved surface is proportional to time (Prop. LV, Theor. XIX)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body moves on a curved surface whose axis passes through the centre of forces, and from the body a perpendicular to the axis is dropped and a parallel to that perpendicular through a fixed axis point is drawn, then that parallel (as it is swept by the radius OP) describes an area proportional to the time of motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up the surface and axes, decompose the central force into components acting in and perpendicular to the surface; resolve the force components and show the in-plane (parallel) component governs motion in the axial plane and produces equal proportionality between incremental arc motion and the corresponding increment of the area described by the radius OP in the auxiliary plane. Thus area AOP (with OP described by the radius in the auxiliary plane) is proportional to elapsed time.
